There are two possibilities regarding the accusative case of "zukhruf." The first: its meaning is: We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, for their houses, a roof of silver and of zukhruf. Since it is not repeated, it is put in the accusative by treating the verb as governing it, and its sense is: as if it were said: "and zukhruf, that is made for them from it." The second possibility: it is conjoined to "the couches," so its meaning is: We would have made these things for them of silver, and We would have made for them, in addition to that, gold which would be for them a wealth by which they become rich. Had the revelation come with the genitive for "zukhruf," it would read: "We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, for their houses, a roof of silver and of zukhruf," so zukhruf would be conjoined to the silver.

And if it had been pluralized as "ma'arij," it would have been correct, just as "miftah" is pluralized as "mafatih," since its singular is mi'raj.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 43, verses 36–37:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he is to him a companion﴾ [36] ﴿And indeed they hinder them from the way, while they think that they are guided﴾ [37]

Says God, may His remembrance be exalted: "And whoever turns away from the remembrance of God, not fearing His might and not dreading His punishment," ﴿We appoint for him a devil, and he is to him a companion﴾. He says: We make for him a devil who misleads him, and he is to him a companion; he says: he is a companion to the devil, meaning he becomes so.

The original meaning of al-'ashw (ʿashw, "turning away/looking") is looking without certainty because of a defect in the eye. It is said of it: ʿasha fulan yaʿshu ʿashwan wa-ʿushuwwan, when his sight weakens and his eye darkens, as if there were a veil over it, as the poet said:

"Whenever you come to him, going about toward the light of his fire, you will find firewood of good quality and a fire blazing."

[This is a verse composed of two halves taken from two different verses. Its first half belongs to al-Hutay'a, from a qasida in praise of Baghid ibn ʿAmir ibn Shammas ibn Lay ibn Anf al-Naqa al-Tamimi. Its second half is from a verse by ʿAbd ibn al-Hurr from a qasida he composed while imprisoned by Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr in Kufa. The full verse of al-Hutay'a, as in (Khizanat al-Adab al-Kabir by al-Baghdadi, 3: 662), is: "Whenever you come to him, going about toward the light of his fire, you will find the best fire, and with it the best of kindlers." The full verse of ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Hurr, as in (al-Khizana 3: 663), is: "Whenever you come to us, visiting us in our homes, you will find firewood of good quality and a fire blazing."

The author cites the verse at His saying: (And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful). Abu ʿUbayda said in Majaz al-Qur'an (folio 220): That is, his eye darkens with respect to it, as if there were a veil over it. Al-Farra' said in Maʿani al-Qur'an (folio 295): He means: whoever turns away from it. As for the one who reads (wa-man yaʿsh) with a fatha on the shin, its meaning is: whoever becomes blind to it. Ibn Qutayba said (Lisan: ʿashiya) that the meaning of His saying (And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful) is that his sight is darkened, and he said: this is the view of Abu ʿUbayda. Then he went on to refute al-Farra's view, saying: I have not seen anyone permit it: ʿashawtu ʿan al-shay' means "I turned away from the thing." It is only said: taʿayashtu ʿan al-shay', meaning I feigned ignorance of it, as if I had not seen it. And likewise taʿamaytu. He said: ʿashawtu ila al-nar means I sought guidance to it by weak sight. Al-Azhari, refuting the words of Ibn Qutayba, said: Ibn Qutayba overlooked the correct position, and despite his oversight he objected to al-Farra'. The Arabs say: ʿashawtu ila al-nar, a-ʿshu ʿashwan, meaning I headed toward it seeking guidance, and ʿashawtu ʿanha, meaning I turned away from it. Thus they distinguish between ila and ʿan when attached to the verb. End.]] That is: "Whenever you are in need and come to him, he will benefit you."

As for when the sight is gone and one does not see, it is said of him: ʿashiya fulan yaʿsha ʿashan, with a shortened form, and from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"She saw a man absent in both his eyes, altered in form, a blind man, a-'sha."

[This verse is by al-A'sha ibn Qays ibn Tha'laba, Maymun ibn Qays (his Diwan, Cairo edition, p. 95). The pronoun in "ra'at" refers to a woman mentioned from the beginning of the poem, whom he named Layla. "Al-wafidan" are the two eyes. "Mukhtalif al-khalq" means that age and the passing years have changed him from the freshness and strength he had known. Al-a'sha is one who has a defect in his eyes, or one who cannot see at night, or one who is blind; the last is the closest meaning given his following word "dariran" (blind). Its verb is ʿashiya yaʿsha ʿasha, like ʿamiya yaʿma. It is different from ʿasha ila al-shay' yaʿsha, when one looks at it and approaches it, or ʿasha ʿanhu yaʿsha ʿashan, when one turns away from it, as we explained in the witness before it. End.]]

From it one says: a man is a-ʿshā (a man with weak sight), and a woman is ʿashwā'.

The meaning of the statement is: whoever does not look into the proofs of God except with a weak glance, turning away from them, like one whose sight has become dim, ﴿We appoint for him a devil﴾. Those who interpret the Qur'an have said things similar to what we have said.

Mention of those who said this:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil﴾, he says: when he turns away from the remembrance of God, We appoint for him a devil ﴿and he is to him a companion﴾.

Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾, he said: turns away.

Some have interpreted it with the meaning: "whoever becomes blind (ya'mā)." Whoever interprets it this way should have the reading ﴿wa-man ya'sh﴾ with a fatha on the shin, according to what I have explained.

Mention of one who interpreted it so: Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾, he said: whoever becomes blind to the remembrance of the Most Merciful.

And His saying: ﴿And indeed they hinder them from the way﴾

Says God, may His remembrance be exalted: And indeed the devils hinder those who turn away from the remembrance of God from the way of truth, adorning error for them and making faith in God and acting in obedience to Him hateful to them. ﴿And they think that they are guided﴾: that is, the polytheists, through the adornment of the devils, suppose that the error they are upon is correct and right; God, exalted is His remembrance, informs that they are upon doubt and without insight in the polytheism in which they are. And He, glorified is His praise, said: ﴿And indeed they hinder them from the way﴾, using a plural form for them, though the reference was earlier singular in ﴿We appoint for him a devil﴾, because the word "shaytan" is singular in form but has the sense of plural.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 43, verse 38–39:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Until, when he comes to Us, he will say, "Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts! What an evil companion!"﴾ (38) ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged, that you are, in the punishment, sharing [it]﴾ (39)

The reciters differed over the reading of His words ﴿Until, when he comes to Us﴾. The majority of the reciters of the Hijaz, except Ibn Muhaysin, and some of the Kufans and some of the Syrians read it as "حتى إذا جاءنا" (hatta idha jaana, with the singular), meaning: until, when there comes to Us this one who was blind to the remembrance of the Most Merciful, and his companion whom Satans were assigned to him. The majority of the reciters of Kufa and Basra, and Ibn Muhaysin, read it as ﴿Until, when he comes to Us﴾ in the singular, meaning: until, when there comes to Us this blind one among the sons of Adam, from the remembrance of the Most Merciful.

The correct view on this matter, in our opinion, is that they are two readings close in meaning. This is because in God's, blessed and exalted is He, report about the state of one of the two parties upon its arrival before Him, regarding what they were paired in during the world, there is sufficiency for the listener about the report of the other, since the report about the state of one of them makes the state of the other known. And they are, besides that, two widely transmitted readings among the readers of the cities, so whichever of them the reader recites, he is correct.

In accordance with what we have said on this, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have spoken.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "Until, when he comes to Us" — he and his companion together.

* *

As for His words: ﴿Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts!﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: one of these two companions said to his other companion: I wish that between me and you were the distance of the two easts, i.e., the distance between the east and the west. The name of one of them was given precedence over the other, as it is said "the two moons" (shabb al-qamarayn), and as the poet said:

"We took by the horizons of the sky over you, / for us are its two moons and the rising stars."

[The verse is by al-Farazdaq (his Diwan, Sawi edition, 519). He said: "its two moons": the sun and the moon, dual-formed by way of precedence. Al-Mubarrad narrated it in al-Kamil: "akhadhna bi-atraf" in one place, and in another place "bi-afaq". End. The author cited it at His words (ya layta bayni wa baynaka ba'da al-mashriqayn): i.e., the distance between the east and the west. He took his speech from al-Farra's speech in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (folio 295). Al-Farra said: he means what is between the east of winter and the east of summer. It is said that he meant the east and the west, and said "al-mashriqayn," and this is the more likely of the two views to be correct; for the Arabs do sometimes combine two names, by naming the more famous of them, so it is said: "the two Zahdams" (jā'aka al-zahdamān), though one of them is Zahm (and the other: Kurdam al-'Absiyan, as mentioned in an earlier witness). And the poet said: "We took by the horizons of the sky..." the verse.]

And as another said:

"So the port of al-Azd is from us, and Iraq is ours, / and the two Mosuls, and from us is Egypt and the Hijaz."

[This witness has the same meaning as the previous one. Al-Farra also cited it in Ma'ani al-Qur'an, like the preceding, to show that two things differing in wording may be combined under one word, so one says "al-Basratan" (the two Basras: Basra and Kufa), and "al-Mawsilan" (the two Mosuls: Mosul and al-Jazira). All of this is of the type of giving precedence to the more famous of the two wordings over the other. He said: a man from Tayy recited to me: "fa-basrat al-Azd minna..." the verse, meaning al-Jazira and Mosul.]

That is, Mosul and al-Jazira; he said "al-Mawsilan," giving precedence to Mosul.

It has also been said that by His words ﴿the distance of the two easts﴾ He means the east of winter and the east of summer, because the sun rises in winter from one east and in summer from another east; likewise the west, it sets in two different wests, as His words, majestic is His praise, say: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾.

It has been mentioned that this is the statement of one of them to the other when each of them is bound to the other until he brings him into Hell.

Mention of those who said that:

Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Sa'id al-Jurayri, who said: It has reached me that when the disbeliever is raised from his grave on the Day of Resurrection, the Satan seizes his hand and does not part from him until God brings the two of them into the Fire. That is when he says: "Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts! What an evil companion!" As for the believer, an angel is assigned to him, and he is with him until... he said: either He separates between the people, or we arrive at what God wills.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 43, verses 40–42:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then can you make the deaf hear, or guide the blind and those who are in manifest error?﴾ (40) ﴿So whether We take you away, indeed We will take retribution from them,﴾ (41) ﴿or We show you that which We have promised them, for indeed We are Able over them.﴾ (42)

He, mention of Him be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Then can you make the deaf hear﴾: [i.e., one] whom Allah has deprived of hearing His proofs with which He argued in this Book, so He has made him deaf to it; ﴿or guide the blind﴾ [i.e., guide to the path of guidance] one whose heart Allah has blinded from seeing, and whom Satan has overcome, so he makes destruction seem fair to him. ﴿And those who are in manifest error﴾ means: or guide those who are in deviation from the right path, following a way other than the way of truth, whose error has made clear that they have strayed from the truth and deviated from the straight path. He, may His praise be exalted, says: That is not up to you; rather, that belongs to Allah, in whose hand is the turning of the hearts of His creatures as He wills. You are only a warner, so convey the warning to them.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿So whether We take you away, indeed We will take retribution from them﴾

The interpreters differed regarding those meant by this threat. Some of them said: it refers to the people of Islam from the community of our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

Those who said this:

- Sawwar ibn ʿAbd Allah al-ʿAnbari narrated to us, he said: my father related to me, from Abu al-Ashhab, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿So whether We take you away, indeed We will take retribution from them﴾, he said: Indeed there was a severe retribution after the Prophet of Allah, so Allah, may His praise be exalted, honoured His Prophet ﷺ by not showing him what retribution would befall his community after him.

- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿So whether We take you away, indeed We will take retribution from them﴾: Allah took His Prophet ﷺ, and he did not see in his community except what would gladden his eye, while Allah left retribution after him. There is no prophet except that he has seen punishment among his community, or he said: what he did not desire. It was mentioned to us that the Prophet ﷺ was shown what his community would suffer after him, and he was never seen but withdrawn, never seen laughing and at ease until he met Allah, blessed and exalted is He.

- Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Maʿmar, he said: Qatadah recited ﴿So whether We take you away, indeed We will take retribution from them﴾ and said: The Prophet ﷺ departed and retribution remained. Allah did not show His Prophet ﷺ anything in his community that he disliked until he passed away; there was never a prophet except that he saw punishment among his community, except your Prophet ﷺ. He said: It was mentioned to us that the Prophet ﷺ was shown what would befall his community after him, and he was not seen laughing and at ease until Allah took him.

Others said: rather, it refers to the polytheists of Quraysh, and they said: Allah has shown His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, [the outcome] regarding them.

Those who said this:

- Muhammad narrated to us, he said: Ahmad narrated to us, he said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His saying: ﴿So whether We take you away, indeed We will take retribution from them﴾, as We took retribution from the past nations. ﴿Or We show you that which We have promised them﴾: Allah indeed showed him that and made him victorious over them.

This second opinion is the more correct of the two interpretations, because this verse occurs within the context of Allah's report about the polytheists, so that it be a threat to them is more fitting than that it be a warning to someone who has not been mentioned. The meaning of the speech, given that this is so, is: If We take you away, O Muhammad, from among these polytheists, bringing you out from amongst them, ﴿indeed We will take retribution from them﴾, as We did with others among the nations that denied their messengers. ﴿Or We show you that which We have promised them﴾, O Muhammad, of victory over them and your elevation above them, ﴿indeed We are Able over them﴾ to make you prevail over them and to humiliate them at your hand and the hands of the believers in you.

**Commentary on the interpretation of God's words, the Exalted:** ﴿So hold fast to what has been revealed to you. Indeed, you are upon a straight path (ṣirāṭ mustaqīm). (43) And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people, and you will be questioned. (44)﴾

God, exalted is His remembrance, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): So hold fast, O Muhammad, to what this Qur'an, which your Lord has revealed to you, commands you. ﴿Indeed, you are upon a straight path﴾ and a sound course. This is the religion of God which He commanded, and it is Islam.

As follows:

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿So hold fast to what has been revealed to you. Indeed, you are upon a straight path﴾: meaning, Islam.

⁕ Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿So hold fast to what has been revealed to you. Indeed, you are upon a straight path﴾.

* *

As for His words: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾

God, exalted is His remembrance, says: And indeed, this Qur'an which has been revealed to you, O Muhammad, which We commanded you to hold fast to, is an honour for you and for your people of Quraysh. ﴿And you will be questioned﴾: meaning, your Lord will question you and them about what you did in it, whether you acted upon what your Lord commanded you in it, and refrained from what He forbade you in it.

The ahl al-ta'wil (the exegetes of the Qur'an) said in agreement with what we have said regarding its interpretation.

Those who said so:

⁕ Ali narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, he said: It means that the Qur'an is an honour for you.

⁕ Amr ibn Malik narrated to me, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, he said: It is said to a man: "Who are you?" He says: "From the Arabs." It is said: "Which of the Arabs?" He says: "From Quraysh."

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾: it is this Qur'an.

⁕ Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, he said: It is an honour for you and your people, meaning the Qur'an.

⁕ Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, he said: Was not prophethood, and the Qur'an revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ), a reminder for him and for his people?

**Commentary on the interpretation of God's words, the Exalted:** ﴿So hold fast to what has been revealed to you. Indeed, you are upon a straight path (ṣirāṭ mustaqīm). (43) And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people, and you will be questioned. (44)﴾

God, exalted is His remembrance, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): So hold fast, O Muhammad, to what this Qur'an, which your Lord has revealed to you, commands you. ﴿Indeed, you are upon a straight path﴾ and a sound course. This is the religion of God which He commanded, and it is Islam.

As follows:

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿So hold fast to what has been revealed to you. Indeed, you are upon a straight path﴾: meaning, Islam.

⁕ Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿So hold fast to what has been revealed to you. Indeed, you are upon a straight path﴾.

* *

As for His words: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾

God, exalted is His remembrance, says: And indeed, this Qur'an which has been revealed to you, O Muhammad, which We commanded you to hold fast to, is an honour for you and for your people of Quraysh. ﴿And you will be questioned﴾: meaning, your Lord will question you and them about what you did in it, whether you acted upon what your Lord commanded you in it, and refrained from what He forbade you in it.

The ahl al-ta'wil (the exegetes of the Qur'an) said in agreement with what we have said regarding its interpretation.

Those who said so:

⁕ Ali narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, he said: It means that the Qur'an is an honour for you.

⁕ Amr ibn Malik narrated to me, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, he said: It is said to a man: "Who are you?" He says: "From the Arabs." It is said: "Which of the Arabs?" He says: "From Quraysh."

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾: it is this Qur'an.

⁕ Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, he said: It is an honour for you and your people, meaning the Qur'an.

⁕ Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, he said: Was not prophethood, and the Qur'an revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ), a reminder for him and for his people?

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 43, verse 45:

The discussion of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers: Did We appoint gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?﴾ (43:45)

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of His saying: ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾ and who it is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was commanded to ask. Some of them said: those whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was commanded to ask are the believers among the People of the Two Books: the Torah and the Gospel.

Mention of those who said this:

Abd al-A'la ibn Wasil narrated to me, saying: Yahya ibn Adam narrated to us, from Ibn Uyaynah, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: In the recitation of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "And ask those to whom We sent Our messengers before you."

Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾: It is the recitation of Abdullah: "Ask those to whom We sent Our messengers before you."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾, he said: Ask the people of the Torah and the Gospel: Did not the messengers come to them with monotheism, that they should affirm God alone? He said: And in some recitations: "And ask those to whom We sent Our messengers before you."  ﴿Did We appoint gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?﴾

Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding some letters: "And ask those to whom We sent Our messengers before you." He said: Ask the People of the Book: Did the messengers not come to them with tawhid? Did they not come with sincere devotion?

It was related to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say, concerning His saying ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾, in the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "Ask those who read the Book before you," meaning: the believers among the People of the Book.

Others said: Rather, those whom he was commanded to ask were the prophets who were gathered for him on the night he was taken on the Night Journey to Bayt al-Maqdis.

Mention of those who said this:

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His saying ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you﴾ ... the verse, he said: They were gathered for him on the night he was taken on the Night Journey to Bayt al-Maqdis, and he led them in prayer. Then God said to him: Ask them. He said: He was more intense in faith and certainty in God, and in what came from God, than to ask them. He recited ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who read the Book before you﴾ and said: So he was not in doubt, and he did not ask the prophets, nor those who read the Book. He said: Gabriel (peace be upon him) called out, and I said to myself: "Now our father Abraham will lead us in prayer." He said: "Gabriel pushed me in the back," [and said]: Advance, O Muhammad, and pray. And he recited ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque﴾ ... until ﴿that We might show him of Our signs﴾.

The most correct of the two opinions regarding the interpretation of this is the view of those who said: what is meant is: ask the believers among the People of the Two Books.

If someone says: How is it permissible to say "ask the messengers" and mean "ask the believers in them and in their books"? It is said: This is permissible because the believers in them and in their books are those who convey to us what they brought from their Lord. So reporting about them and about what they brought from their Lord, when it is authentic, has the sense of asking them, and asking about what they brought has the sense of asking them when the one asked is knowledgeable about them and truthful regarding them. This is akin to the command of Allah, the Majestic and Praised, to us to refer what we dispute to Allah and to the Messenger, when He says: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾. It is well known that the meaning of this is: refer it to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, because referring to these is referring to Allah and the Messenger. Likewise His saying: ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾ means only: ask the books of those messengers whom We sent before you, for you know the authenticity of that from Us, so mention of the messengers suffices in place of mention of the books, since the meaning is known.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿Did We appoint gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?﴾

It means: Did We command them to worship gods other than Allah in what they brought them, or did they bring them the command to that from Us?

Those among the exegetes who speak in agreement with what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said this:

Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿Did We appoint gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?﴾: Did the messengers come to them commanding them to worship gods other than Allah?

It was said: ﴿gods to be worshipped﴾ — the report about the gods is given in the form of a report about male sons of Adam, and it does not say "tu'bad" or "yu'badna," which would make it feminine, though they are stones, or some inanimate objects, as is done when reporting about some inanimate objects. Rather, it was done this way because they were worshipped and venerated in the manner people venerate their kings and nobles, so the report about them was treated as a report about the owned and the nobles among the sons of Adam.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 43, verses 46–47:

The exegesis (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, so he said, "Indeed, I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." (46) But when he brought them Our signs, at once they laughed at them.﴾ (47)

Say, may His remembrance be exalted: And We certainly sent Musa, O Muhammad, with Our proofs to Pharaoh and the nobles of his people, just as We sent you to these polytheists of your people. Musa said to them, "Indeed, I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds," just as you said to your people of Quraysh: "Indeed, I am the messenger of God to you."

﴿But when he brought them Our signs, at once they laughed at them﴾: meaning, when Musa came to Pharaoh and his chiefs with Our proofs and evidences of the truth of his words, in what he called them to, namely the oneness of God and disavowal of worshipping idols, at once Pharaoh and his people laughed at what Musa brought them of signs and lessons; just as your people mock what you have brought them of signs and lessons. This is a consolation from God, exalted and majestic, to His Prophet ﷺ regarding what he suffered from the polytheists of his people, and an informing from Him to him that his people, being of the people of polytheism, will be no different from the other nations who followed their path in disbelief in God and denial of His messengers. It is also an exhortation from Him to His Prophet ﷺ to follow the example of patience with them set by the messengers of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm), and an informing from Him to him that the end of their rebelliousness is ruin and destruction, in accordance with His practice toward those who rebelled against Him before them, and His granting him victory over them and the elevation of His command, as He did with Musa, peace be upon him, and his people who believed in him, by making them triumph over Pharaoh and his chiefs.

The Interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We showed them no sign but it was greater than its fellow, and We seized them with punishment that they might return.﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: We did not show Pharaoh and his chiefs any sign, meaning a proof from Us against them of the truth of what Our messenger Moses calls them to, ﴿but it was greater than its fellow﴾, meaning: except that the one We showed them was greater in proof against them and more emphatic than the signs that came before it, and more indicative of the truth of what Moses commanded them concerning the oneness of God.

* *

As for His words: ﴿And We seized them with punishment﴾

He says: We sent down punishment upon them, like His seizing them with years of drought, and loss of fruits, and with locusts, lice, frogs, and blood.

* *

As for His words: ﴿that they might return﴾

He says: that they might turn back from their disbelief in God to His oneness and obedience, and repent of the sins in which they persisted.

As follows:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿And We seized them with punishment that they might return﴾: i.e., that they might repent, or be mindful.

On the interpretation of His words, "And they said, 'O you who practice magic, call upon your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you. Indeed, we will be guided.' But when We removed from them the punishment, behold, they broke their word."

Allah, the Exalted, says: Pharaoh and his chiefs said to Musa, "O you who practice magic, call upon your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you." By their saying "by what He has covenanted with you," they meant: by His covenant which He made with you, that if we believe in you and follow you, the plague would be removed from us.

As narrated to us:

Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, "by what He has covenanted with you," he said: "If we believe, He will surely remove the punishment from us."

If someone says to us: What is the meaning of their saying, "O you who practice magic, call upon your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you," and how did they call him a magician while they were asking him to call upon his Lord for them to remove the punishment from them? It is said: The word "sahir" (magician) meant among them "the learned one," and magic was not blameworthy in their view; they addressed him by this title because its meaning among them was: "O you who are learned."

* *

And regarding His words, "Indeed, we will be guided."

He means: they said, "Indeed, we will follow you, affirming you in what you have brought us, and we will affirm Allah's oneness, and we will see the path of right guidance."

The people of interpretation have said the same as what we have said on this matter.

Those who said that:

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words, "O you who practice magic, call upon your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you. Indeed, we will be guided," he said: They said, "O Musa, call upon your Lord for us; if you remove the plague from us, we will surely believe in you."

* *

And regarding His words, "But when We removed from them the punishment, behold, they broke their word."

Allah, the Exalted, says: When We lifted from them the punishment which We had sent down upon them, the punishment which they had promised that if it were removed from them they would be guided to the path of truth, behold, after We removed it from them they break the covenant they had made with Us; that is, they betray and persist in their misguidance and continue in their error.

The people of interpretation have said the same as what we have said on this matter.

Those who said that:

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, "behold, they break their word": i.e., they betray.

On the interpretation of His words, "And they said, 'O you who practice magic, call upon your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you. Indeed, we will be guided.' But when We removed from them the punishment, behold, they broke their word."

Those who said that:

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, "behold, they break their word": i.e., they betray.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 43, verse 51:

The explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people, saying, "O my people, does not the dominion of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Then do you not see?"﴾ (43:51)

His saying, exalted is His remembrance: ﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people﴾ from the Copts, so ﴿he said, "O my people, does not the dominion of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Then do you not see?"﴾. By His saying ﴿beneath me﴾ he means: before me, in the gardens.

As related:

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿and these rivers flowing beneath me﴾, he said: They had gardens and rivers of water.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿Then do you not see?﴾

He means: Then do you not see, O people, what I am in of bliss and goodness, and what Moses is in of poverty and a stammering tongue? The enemy of God boasted of his kingdom over Egypt and of what had been granted him of the world as a respite from God for him, and he supposed that what he was in of that he had attained by his own hand and power, and that Moses had only failed to attain what he described. So he disparaged him on that account, arguing against the ignorant among his people that if Moses were truthful in what he brought of signs and lessons, and it were not sorcery, he would have acquired for himself kingdom and blessing like what Pharaoh was in of that, but (Pharaoh said this) out of ignorance of God and deception by His leniency toward him.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 43, verses 52–53:

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Am ana khayrun min hadha alladhi huwa mahin wa la yakadu yubin﴾ [Am ana khayrun min hadha alladhi huwa mahin wa la yakadu yubin] (52) ﴿Falawla ulqiya alayhi asawiratun min dhahabin aw ja'a ma'ahu al-malaikatu muqtarinin﴾ (53)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says, relating the statement of Pharaoh to his people after he had argued against them with his kingdom and authority, the eloquence of his speech, the perfection of his form, and the superiority of himself over Moses by the attributes with which he described himself and Moses: "I am better, O people, and my description is this description which I have described to you. ﴿Or is this one who is despised﴾, who possesses no kingdom or wealth, with the defect in his body and the affliction in his tongue, so that he can hardly make his speech clear?"

Scholars have differed concerning the meaning of His words ﴿Am﴾ in this place. Some of them said: its meaning is "Rather, I am better," and they said: "That is better," not as an interrogative.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad narrated to us: he said: Ahmad narrated to us: he said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿Am ana khayrun min hadha alladhi huwa mahin﴾: He said: "Rather, I am better than this one."

Some scholars of the Arabic language from the people of Basra used to say something similar to this.

Some grammarians of Kufa said: it is of the interrogative form which is introduced by "am," because it is connected to the speech before it. He said: "If you wish, you may refer it to His words: ﴿Is not the kingdom of Egypt mine?﴾" When the speech is directed to being an interrogative, there must be an omitted element in the speech, dispensed with by what is mentioned of what its mention has been left out, and the meaning of the speech then becomes: "I am better, O people, than this one who is despised, or is he?"

It has been reported from some reciters that he used to read it as "Amma ana khayrun" [أما أنا خَيْرٌ].

Al-Farra' narrated this to us, saying: Some elders informed me that it reached them that some reciters read it thus. Had this reading been widely transmitted among the reciters of the cities, it would have been sound, and its meaning would have been good; however, it differs from what the reciters of the cities hold, so I do not permit reciting by it. And upon this reading, if it were sound, there is no difficulty in its meaning nor any burden.

The correct recitation in this matter is what the reciters of the cities hold. The most fitting of the interpretations of the speech, given that this is the case, is the interpretation of one who takes "am ana khayrun" as an interrogative introduced by "am," connected to what precedes it in speech, and directs it to mean: "Am I better than this one who is despised? Or is he?" Then the mention of "am huwa" is omitted, because of the indication in the speech pointing to it.

By His words ﴿min hadha alladhi huwa mahin﴾ is meant: from this one who is weak, due to the scarcity of his wealth, and that he does not possess the kingdom and authority that I possess.

Scholars of interpretation have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿Am ana khayrun min hadha alladhi huwa mahin﴾: He said: "Weak."

Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿min hadha alladhi huwa mahin﴾: He said: "Mahin: the weak."

* *

And His words ﴿wa la yakadu yubin﴾:

He says: and he can hardly make speech clear because of the impediment of his tongue. Scholars of interpretation have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿wa la yakadu yubin﴾: i.e., impeded of tongue.

Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿wa la yakadu yubin﴾: the speech.

* *

And His words ﴿Falawla ulqiya alayhi asawiratun min dhahabin﴾:

He says: "Why then was it not cast upon Moses, if he is truthful that he is the messenger of the Lord of the worlds, bracelets of gold?" It is the plural of siwar, which is the bangle worn on the arm.

Scholars of interpretation have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿asawiratun min dhahabin﴾: He says: "Bracelets of gold."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿asawiratun min dhahabin﴾: i.e., bracelets of gold.

The reciters differed in the recitation of this. The common reciters of Madinah, Basra and Kufa recited it as "Falawla ulqiya alayhi asawiratun min dhahabin" [أَسَاوِرَةٌ]. It has been reported from al-Hasan al-Basri that he used to recite it as ﴿asawiratun min dhahabin﴾.

The more fitting of the two readings in my view is what the reciters of the cities hold, although the other is sound in meaning.

The grammarians of Arabic differed concerning the singular of asawira and asawira. Some Basran grammarians said: asawira is the plural of isawar, and asawira is the plural of asawira. He said: whoever reads it as asawira, he meant asawir, and God knows best, so he made the ha' a substitute for the ya', like zanadiqa, in which the ha' became a substitute for the ya' in zanadiq. Some Kufan grammarians said: whoever reads asawira makes its singular isawar; whoever reads asawira makes its singular siwar. He said: asawira may be the plural of asawira, as is said in the plural of aqiyah being asaqi, and in the plural of akra' being akari'. Another of them said: it has been said of the bracelet of the arm that it may be aswar and isawar; he said: so it is permissible in this dialect that asawira is its plural. It is reported from Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' that he used to say: the singular of asawira is isawar. He said: confirming this is the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: ﴿Falawla ulqiya alayhi asawiratun min dhahabin﴾. If what has been transmitted is correct, that it is permissible to say isawar for the bracelet of the arm, then there is no difficulty in its plural being asawira. I do not know this to be sound from the Arabs by a transmitted report from them, since what is well known in their speech of the meaning of isawar is: the archer, the skilled man in archery among the men of the non-Arabs. As for what is worn on the arm, its well-known name among them is siwar. When this is so, then what is more fitting for asawira is that it be the plural of asawira according to what the one whose statement we have mentioned has said about it.

* *

And His words ﴿aw ja'a ma'ahu al-malaikatu muqtarinin﴾:

He says: "Or why not, if he is truthful, did the angels come with him, accompanying one another, following one another, bearing witness for him that he is the messenger of God to them?" Scholars of interpretation, with differences among them in the expression of its interpretation, have said something similar to what we have said regarding this. Some of them said: "They walk together."

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, Abu Asim said, Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them, from Ibn Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿al-malaikatu muqtarinin﴾: He said: "They walk together."

Others said: "Following one another."

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Zayd narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿aw ja'a ma'ahu al-malaikatu muqtarinin﴾: i.e., following one another.

Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, the like of it.

Others said: "They accompany one another."

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿aw ja'a ma'ahu al-malaikatu muqtarinin﴾: He said: "They accompany one another."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 43, verses 52–53:

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Am ana khayrun min hadha alladhi huwa mahin wa la yakadu yubin﴾ [Am ana khayrun min hadha alladhi huwa mahin wa la yakadu yubin] (52) ﴿Falawla ulqiya alayhi asawiratun min dhahabin aw ja'a ma'ahu al-malaikatu muqtarinin﴾ (53)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says, relating the statement of Pharaoh to his people after he had argued against them with his kingdom and authority, the eloquence of his speech, the perfection of his form, and the superiority of himself over Moses by the attributes with which he described himself and Moses: "I am better, O people, and my description is this description which I have described to you. ﴿Or is this one who is despised﴾, who possesses no kingdom or wealth, with the defect in his body and the affliction in his tongue, so that he can hardly make his speech clear?"

Scholars have differed concerning the meaning of His words ﴿Am﴾ in this place. Some of them said: its meaning is "Rather, I am better," and they said: "That is better," not as an interrogative.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad narrated to us: he said: Ahmad narrated to us: he said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿Am ana khayrun min hadha alladhi huwa mahin﴾: He said: "Rather, I am better than this one."

Some scholars of the Arabic language from the people of Basra used to say something similar to this.

Some grammarians of Kufa said: it is of the interrogative form which is introduced by "am," because it is connected to the speech before it. He said: "If you wish, you may refer it to His words: ﴿Is not the kingdom of Egypt mine?﴾" When the speech is directed to being an interrogative, there must be an omitted element in the speech, dispensed with by what is mentioned of what its mention has been left out, and the meaning of the speech then becomes: "I am better, O people, than this one who is despised, or is he?"

It has been reported from some reciters that he used to read it as "Amma ana khayrun" [أما أنا خَيْرٌ].

Al-Farra' narrated this to us, saying: Some elders informed me that it reached them that some reciters read it thus. Had this reading been widely transmitted among the reciters of the cities, it would have been sound, and its meaning would have been good; however, it differs from what the reciters of the cities hold, so I do not permit reciting by it. And upon this reading, if it were sound, there is no difficulty in its meaning nor any burden.

The correct recitation in this matter is what the reciters of the cities hold. The most fitting of the interpretations of the speech, given that this is the case, is the interpretation of one who takes "am ana khayrun" as an interrogative introduced by "am," connected to what precedes it in speech, and directs it to mean: "Am I better than this one who is despised? Or is he?" Then the mention of "am huwa" is omitted, because of the indication in the speech pointing to it.

By His words ﴿min hadha alladhi huwa mahin﴾ is meant: from this one who is weak, due to the scarcity of his wealth, and that he does not possess the kingdom and authority that I possess.

Scholars of interpretation have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿Am ana khayrun min hadha alladhi huwa mahin﴾: He said: "Weak."

Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿min hadha alladhi huwa mahin﴾: He said: "Mahin: the weak."

* *

And His words ﴿wa la yakadu yubin﴾:

He says: and he can hardly make speech clear because of the impediment of his tongue. Scholars of interpretation have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿wa la yakadu yubin﴾: i.e., impeded of tongue.

Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿wa la yakadu yubin﴾: the speech.

* *

And His words ﴿Falawla ulqiya alayhi asawiratun min dhahabin﴾:

He says: "Why then was it not cast upon Moses, if he is truthful that he is the messenger of the Lord of the worlds, bracelets of gold?" It is the plural of siwar, which is the bangle worn on the arm.

Scholars of interpretation have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿asawiratun min dhahabin﴾: He says: "Bracelets of gold."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿asawiratun min dhahabin﴾: i.e., bracelets of gold.

The reciters differed in the recitation of this. The common reciters of Madinah, Basra and Kufa recited it as "Falawla ulqiya alayhi asawiratun min dhahabin" [أَسَاوِرَةٌ]. It has been reported from al-Hasan al-Basri that he used to recite it as ﴿asawiratun min dhahabin﴾.

The more fitting of the two readings in my view is what the reciters of the cities hold, although the other is sound in meaning.

The grammarians of Arabic differed concerning the singular of asawira and asawira. Some Basran grammarians said: asawira is the plural of isawar, and asawira is the plural of asawira. He said: whoever reads it as asawira, he meant asawir, and God knows best, so he made the ha' a substitute for the ya', like zanadiqa, in which the ha' became a substitute for the ya' in zanadiq. Some Kufan grammarians said: whoever reads asawira makes its singular isawar; whoever reads asawira makes its singular siwar. He said: asawira may be the plural of asawira, as is said in the plural of aqiyah being asaqi, and in the plural of akra' being akari'. Another of them said: it has been said of the bracelet of the arm that it may be aswar and isawar; he said: so it is permissible in this dialect that asawira is its plural. It is reported from Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' that he used to say: the singular of asawira is isawar. He said: confirming this is the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: ﴿Falawla ulqiya alayhi asawiratun min dhahabin﴾. If what has been transmitted is correct, that it is permissible to say isawar for the bracelet of the arm, then there is no difficulty in its plural being asawira. I do not know this to be sound from the Arabs by a transmitted report from them, since what is well known in their speech of the meaning of isawar is: the archer, the skilled man in archery among the men of the non-Arabs. As for what is worn on the arm, its well-known name among them is siwar. When this is so, then what is more fitting for asawira is that it be the plural of asawira according to what the one whose statement we have mentioned has said about it.

* *

Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿aw ja'a ma'ahu al-malaikatu muqtarinin﴾: He said: "They accompany one another."

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he made light of his people, and they obeyed him. Indeed, they were a defiantly disobedient people.﴾ (54) ﴿And when they angered Us, We took retribution from them and drowned them all.﴾ (55)

Says God, may His remembrance be exalted: Pharaoh made light of a group of his people, the Copts, with his statement which God, blessed and exalted is He, reported that he said to them. They accepted that from him and obeyed him, and they denied Musa. God says: They only obeyed and responded to what the enemy of God invited them to, of affirming him and denying Musa, because they were a people outside the obedience of God, abandoned by His forsaking them and His sealing their hearts. God, blessed and exalted is He, says: ﴿When they angered Us﴾. By His saying "angered Us" (āsafūnā) He means: they provoked Us to anger.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said something similar to what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

- ʿAlī narrated to me, who said: Abū Ṣāliḥ narrated to us, who said: Muʿāwiya narrated to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying ﴿When they angered Us﴾: he says: "They provoked Us to wrath" (asakhhaṭūnā).

- Muḥammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, who said: my father narrated to me, who said: my uncle narrated to me, who said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿When they angered Us﴾: he says: "When they made Us angry."

- Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, who said: Abū ʿĀṣim narrated to us, who said: ʿĪsā narrated to us; and al-Ḥārith narrated to me, who said: al-Ḥasan narrated to us, who said: Warqāʾ narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding ﴿When they angered Us﴾: "They angered Us."

- Bishr narrated to us, who said: Yazīd narrated to us, who said: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah, regarding His saying: ﴿When they angered Us﴾, he said: "They angered their Lord."

- Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā narrated to us, who said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah regarding ﴿When they angered Us﴾, he said: "They angered Us."

- Muḥammad narrated to us, who said: Aḥmad narrated to us, who said: Asbāṭ narrated to us, from al-Suddī regarding ﴿When they angered Us﴾, he said: "They angered Us." And it is in the sense of Yaʿqūb's saying: ﴿Alas, my grief for Joseph!﴾, he said: "Oh my sorrow over Joseph."

- Yūnus narrated to me, who said: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿When they angered Us, We took retribution from them﴾, he said: "They angered Us." And His saying ﴿We took retribution from them﴾ means: We took retribution from them with the swift punishment that We hastened for them, and We drowned them all in the sea.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 43, verses 56–57:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿So We made them a precedent and an example for the later ones﴾ (56) ﴿And when the son of Mary was cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it in dismay﴾ (57)

The reciters differed in their reading of this. The majority of the reciters of Kufa, except ʿĀṣim, read "fa-jaʿalnāhum sulufan" with a ḍamma on the sīn and the lām, taking it as the plural of salīf (sulafāʾ, sulaf), meaning one who goes before a people. al-Farrāʾ related that he heard al-Qāsim ibn Maʿn mention that he had heard the Arabs say: "A salīf of the people has passed on." The majority of the reciters of Medina, of Basra, and ʿĀṣim read ﴿fa-jaʿalnāhum salafan﴾ with a fatḥa on the sīn and the lām.

When it is read thus, it may be intended to refer to a group or to an individual, masculine or feminine, since it is said of a people: "You are a salaf for us," and it may be pluralized, so it is said: "hum aslāf." From this is the report related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "The righteous will pass away as salaf (precursors)."

Ḥumayd al-Aʿraj used to read it: "fa-jaʿalnāhum sulafan" with a ḍamma on the sīn and a fatḥa on the lām, taking it as the plural of sulfa from the people, like ummah (a group) among them and qiṭʿah (a piece).

The most correct reading in this matter is the reading of the one who reads it with a fatḥa on the sīn and the lām, because it is the most eloquent dialect and the well-known speech of the Arabs, and the most worthy of the dialects in which the Book of God should be recited is the most eloquent and most widely known among them. The meaning of the statement, then, is: We made those whom We drowned from the people of Pharaoh in the sea a precedent who go before to the Fire, and an example for the disbelievers of your people, O Muhammad, from Quraysh, and for the disbelievers of your people who are to come after them.

The interpreters of the Qur'an have said the like of what we have said.

Those who said so:

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us, saying: ʿĪsā related to us; and al-Ḥārith related to me, saying: al-Ḥasan related to us, saying: Warqāʾ related to us, all of them from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding His saying: ﴿So We made them a precedent and an example for the later ones﴾ He said: The people of Pharaoh, their disbelievers, were a precedent for the disbelievers of the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah: ﴿So We made them a precedent﴾ into the Fire.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar: ﴿So We made them a precedent﴾ He said: a precedent to the Fire.

And His saying: ﴿and an example for the later ones﴾

He means: a lesson and an admonition by which those nations after them may take warning, so that they desist from disbelief in God. The interpreters have said the like of this.

Those who said so:

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us, saying: ʿĪsā related to us; and al-Ḥārith related to me, saying: al-Ḥasan related to us, saying: Warqāʾ related to us, all of them from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid: ﴿and an example for the later ones﴾ He said: a lesson for those after them.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, saying: Abū Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah: ﴿and an example for the later ones﴾: that is, an admonition for the later ones.

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah: ﴿and an example for the later ones﴾: that is, an admonition for those after them.

Muhammad related to us, saying: Aḥmad related to us, saying: Asbāṭ related to us, from al-Suddī: ﴿So We made them a precedent and an example﴾ He said: a lesson.

And His saying: ﴿And when the son of Mary was cited as an example﴾

Almighty God says: When God likened ʿĪsā in his origination and creation, without a father, to Ādam, comparing him to Him in that He created him from dust without a father, your people, O Muhammad, cry out in dismay because of this, and say: Muhammad wants nothing from us except that we take him as a god to worship, just as the Christians worshipped the Messiah.

The interpreters differed in the explanation of this. Some of them said something similar to what we have said.

Those who said so:

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us, saying: ʿĪsā related to us; and al-Ḥārith related to me, saying: al-Ḥasan related to us, saying: Warqāʾ related to us, all of them from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿your people turn away from it in dismay﴾ He said: they cry out. He said: Quraysh said: Muhammad only wants us to worship him as the people of ʿĪsā worshipped ʿĪsā.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, who said: When ʿĪsā the son of Mary was mentioned, Quraysh grew distressed at that and said: O Muhammad, why do you mention ʿĪsā the son of Mary? [[As in the original; the speech is incomplete, and perhaps he relied on what follows to indicate it.]] They said: Muhammad wants nothing but that we do to him what the Christians did to ʿĪsā the son of Mary. Then God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They have not struck it for you except as a dispute﴾.

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah, who said: When ʿĪsā was mentioned in the Qur'an, the polytheists of Quraysh said: O Muhammad, what made you bring up ʿĪsā? He said: And they said: He only wants us to love him as the Christians loved ʿĪsā.

Others said: Rather, by it is meant the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell; you will be its certain entrants﴾. When this was revealed, it was said to the polytheists: We are content that our gods be with ʿĪsā and ʿUzayr and the angels, since all of these are things worshipped besides God. God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And when the son of Mary was cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it in dismay﴾, and they said: Are our gods better, or he?

Those who said so:

Muhammad ibn Saʿd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās: ﴿And when the son of Mary was cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it in dismay﴾ He said: meaning Quraysh, when it was said to them: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell; you will be its certain entrants﴾, Quraysh said to him: Then what of the son of Mary? He said: That is the servant of God and His messenger. They said: By God, this man wants only that we take him as a lord, just as the Christians took ʿĪsā the son of Mary as a lord. God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They have not struck it for you except as a dispute. Nay, they are a contentious people﴾.

The reciters differed in their reading of His saying: ﴿yaṣudduna﴾. The majority of the reciters of Medina and a group of the reciters of Kufa read "yaṣuddūna" with a ḍamma on the ṣād. Some of the reciters of Kufa and Basra read ﴿yaṣiddūna﴾ with a kasra on the ṣād.

The scholars of the Arabic language differed concerning the difference between the two when read with a ḍamma on the ṣād and when read with a kasra. Some grammarians of Basra, and some of the Kufans agreeing with him, said: they are two dialects with one meaning, like yashuddu and yashiddu, and yanummu and yanimmu from al-namīmah (tale-bearing). Another said: whoever read it with a kasra, its meaning is "they cry out," and whoever read it with a ḍamma, its meaning is "they turn away." Some who read it with a kasra said: he intended "they cry out," and whoever read it with a ḍamma intended turning away from the truth.

Ḥudithtu ʿan al-Farrāʾ, who said: Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh related to me, that ʿĀṣim left "yaṣuddūna" from the reading of Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and read "yaṣiddūna," and said: Abū Bakr said: ʿĀṣim related to me, from Abū Razīn, from Abū Yaḥyā, that Ibn ʿAbbās met the nephew of ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and said: Indeed your uncle is an Arab, so why does he err in his saying "idhā qawmuka minhu yaṣuddūna," when it is only "yaṣiddūna"?

The correct view on this matter is that both are well-known readings and two well-known dialects with one meaning. We have not found that the interpreters distinguished between the meaning when it is read with a ḍamma and with a kasra. Had its meaning differed, the disagreement over its interpretation among its people would have existed to the same extent as the disagreement in reading due to the difference of the two dialects. But since its meaning did not differ, they did not disagree that its interpretation is: they cry out and become distressed. So whichever of the two readings the reader recites, he is correct.

Explanation of what we have said regarding its interpretation:

Ali related to me, saying: Abū Ṣāliḥ related to us, saying: Muʿāwiyah related to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: ﴿When your people turn away from it in dismay﴾ He said: they cry out.

Muhammad ibn Saʿd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās: ﴿When your people turn away from it in dismay﴾ He says: they cry out.

Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Wāḍiḥ related to us, saying: Abū Ḥamzah related to us, from al-Mughīrah al-Ḍabbī, from al-Ṣaʿb ibn ʿUthmān, who said: Ibn ʿAbbās used to read ﴿idhā qawmuka minhu yaṣuddūna﴾, and he would explain it by saying: they cry out.

Ibn Bashshār related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us, from ʿĀṣim, from Abū Razīn, from Ibn ʿAbbās: ﴿When your people turn away from it in dismay﴾ He said: they cry out.

Ibn al-Muthannā related to us, saying: Ibn Abī ʿAdī related to us, from Shuʿbah, from ʿĀṣim, from Abū Razīn, from Ibn ʿAbbās, similarly.

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us, saying: ʿĪsā related to us; and al-Ḥārith related to me, saying: al-Ḥasan related to us, saying: Warqāʾ related to us, all of them from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿When your people turn away from it in dismay﴾ He said: they cry out.

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah: ﴿When your people turn away from it in dismay﴾: that is, they become distressed and cry out.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, from ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he read it ﴿yaṣuddūna﴾: that is, they cry out; and ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him) read ﴿yaṣuddūna﴾.

I was told on the authority of al-Ḥusayn, who said: I heard Abū Muʿādh say: ʿUbayd related to us, who said: I heard al-Ḍaḥḥāk say, regarding His saying: ﴿When your people turn away from it in dismay﴾: they cry out.

Muhammad related to us, saying: Aḥmad related to us, saying: Asbāṭ related to us, from al-Suddī: ﴿When your people turn away from it in dismay﴾ He said: they cry out.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 43, verses 56–57:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿So We made them a precedent and an example for the later ones﴾ (56) ﴿And when the son of Mary was cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it in dismay﴾ (57)

The reciters differed in their reading of this. The majority of the reciters of Kufa, except ʿĀṣim, read "fa-jaʿalnāhum sulufan" with a ḍamma on the sīn and the lām, taking it as the plural of salīf (sulafāʾ, sulaf), meaning one who goes before a people. al-Farrāʾ related that he heard al-Qāsim ibn Maʿn mention that he had heard the Arabs say: "A salīf of the people has passed on." The majority of the reciters of Medina, of Basra, and ʿĀṣim read ﴿fa-jaʿalnāhum salafan﴾ with a fatḥa on the sīn and the lām.

When it is read thus, it may be intended to refer to a group or to an individual, masculine or feminine, since it is said of a people: "You are a salaf for us," and it may be pluralized, so it is said: "hum aslāf." From this is the report related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "The righteous will pass away as salaf (precursors)."

Ḥumayd al-Aʿraj used to read it: "fa-jaʿalnāhum sulafan" with a ḍamma on the sīn and a fatḥa on the lām, taking it as the plural of sulfa from the people, like ummah (a group) among them and qiṭʿah (a piece).

The most correct reading in this matter is the reading of the one who reads it with a fatḥa on the sīn and the lām, because it is the most eloquent dialect and the well-known speech of the Arabs, and the most worthy of the dialects in which the Book of God should be recited is the most eloquent and most widely known among them. The meaning of the statement, then, is: We made those whom We drowned from the people of Pharaoh in the sea a precedent who go before to the Fire, and an example for the disbelievers of your people, O Muhammad, from Quraysh, and for the disbelievers of your people who are to come after them.

The interpreters of the Qur'an have said the like of what we have said.

Those who said so:

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us, saying: ʿĪsā related to us; and al-Ḥārith related to me, saying: al-Ḥasan related to us, saying: Warqāʾ related to us, all of them from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding His saying: ﴿So We made them a precedent and an example for the later ones﴾ He said: The people of Pharaoh, their disbelievers, were a precedent for the disbelievers of the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah: ﴿So We made them a precedent﴾ into the Fire.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar: ﴿So We made them a precedent﴾ He said: a precedent to the Fire.

And His saying: ﴿and an example for the later ones﴾

He means: a lesson and an admonition by which those nations after them may take warning, so that they desist from disbelief in God. The interpreters have said the like of this.

Those who said so:

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us, saying: ʿĪsā related to us; and al-Ḥārith related to me, saying: al-Ḥasan related to us, saying: Warqāʾ related to us, all of them from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid: ﴿and an example for the later ones﴾ He said: a lesson for those after them.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, saying: Abū Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah: ﴿and an example for the later ones﴾: that is, an admonition for the later ones.

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah: ﴿and an example for the later ones﴾: that is, an admonition for those after them.

Muhammad related to us, saying: Aḥmad related to us, saying: Asbāṭ related to us, from al-Suddī: ﴿So We made them a precedent and an example﴾ He said: a lesson.

And His saying: ﴿And when the son of Mary was cited as an example﴾

Almighty God says: When God likened ʿĪsā in his origination and creation, without a father, to Ādam, comparing him to Him in that He created him from dust without a father, your people, O Muhammad, cry out in dismay because of this, and say: Muhammad wants nothing from us except that we take him as a god to worship, just as the Christians worshipped the Messiah.

The interpreters differed in the explanation of this. Some of them said something similar to what we have said.

Those who said so:

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us, saying: ʿĪsā related to us; and al-Ḥārith related to me, saying: al-Ḥasan related to us, saying: Warqāʾ related to us, all of them from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿your people turn away from it in dismay﴾ He said: they cry out. He said: Quraysh said: Muhammad only wants us to worship him as the people of ʿĪsā worshipped ʿĪsā.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, who said: When ʿĪsā the son of Mary was mentioned, Quraysh grew distressed at that and said: O Muhammad, why do you mention ʿĪsā the son of Mary? [[As in the original; the speech is incomplete, and perhaps he relied on what follows to indicate it.]] They said: Muhammad wants nothing but that we do to him what the Christians did to ʿĪsā the son of Mary. Then God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They have not struck it for you except as a dispute﴾.

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah, who said: When ʿĪsā was mentioned in the Qur'an, the polytheists of Quraysh said: O Muhammad, what made you bring up ʿĪsā? He said: And they said: He only wants us to love him as the Christians loved ʿĪsā.

Others said: Rather, by it is meant the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell; you will be its certain entrants﴾. When this was revealed, it was said to the polytheists: We are content that our gods be with ʿĪsā and ʿUzayr and the angels, since all of these are things worshipped besides God. God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And when the son of Mary was cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it in dismay﴾, and they said: Are our gods better, or he?

Those who said so:

Muhammad ibn Saʿd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās: ﴿And when the son of Mary was cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it in dismay﴾ He said: meaning Quraysh, when it was said to them: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell; you will be its certain entrants﴾, Quraysh said to him: Then what of the son of Mary? He said: That is the servant of God and His messenger. They said: By God, this man wants only that we take him as a lord, just as the Christians took ʿĪsā the son of Mary as a lord. God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They have not struck it for you except as a dispute. Nay, they are a contentious people﴾.

The reciters differed in their reading of His saying: ﴿yaṣudduna﴾. The majority of the reciters of Medina and a group of the reciters of Kufa read "yaṣuddūna" with a ḍamma on the ṣād. Some of the reciters of Kufa and Basra read ﴿yaṣiddūna﴾ with a kasra on the ṣād.

The scholars of the Arabic language differed concerning the difference between the two when read with a ḍamma on the ṣād and when read with a kasra. Some grammarians of Basra, and some of the Kufans agreeing with him, said: they are two dialects with one meaning, like yashuddu and yashiddu, and yanummu and yanimmu from al-namīmah (tale-bearing). Another said: whoever read it with a kasra, its meaning is "they cry out," and whoever read it with a ḍamma, its meaning is "they turn away." Some who read it with a kasra said: he intended "they cry out," and whoever read it with a ḍamma intended turning away from the truth.

Ḥudithtu ʿan al-Farrāʾ, who said: Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh related to me, that ʿĀṣim left "yaṣuddūna" from the reading of Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and read "yaṣiddūna," and said: Abū Bakr said: ʿĀṣim related to me, from Abū Razīn, from Abū Yaḥyā, that Ibn ʿAbbās met the nephew of ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and said: Indeed your uncle is an Arab, so why does he err in his saying "idhā qawmuka minhu yaṣuddūna," when it is only "yaṣiddūna"?

The correct view on this matter is that both are well-known readings and two well-known dialects with one meaning. We have not found that the interpreters distinguished between the meaning when it is read with a ḍamma and with a kasra. Had its meaning differed, the disagreement over its interpretation among its people would have existed to the same extent as the disagreement in reading due to the difference of the two dialects. But since its meaning did not differ, they did not disagree that its interpretation is: they cry out and become distressed. So whichever of the two readings the reader recites, he is correct.

Explanation of what we have said regarding its interpretation:

Ali related to me, saying: Abū Ṣāliḥ related to us, saying: Muʿāwiyah related to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: ﴿When your people turn away from it in dismay﴾ He said: they cry out.

Muhammad ibn Saʿd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās: ﴿When your people turn away from it in dismay﴾ He says: they cry out.
